prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I shall never get you put together entirely, Pieced, glued, and properly jointed. Mule-bray, pig-grunt and bawdy cackles Proceed from your great lips. It’s worse than a barnyard. Perhaps you consider yourself an oracle, Mouthpiece of the dead, or of some god or other. Thirty years now I have labored To dredge the silt from your throat. I am none the wiser. Scaling little ladders with glue pots and pails of lysol I crawl like an ant in mourning Over the weedy acres of your brow To mend the immense skull plates and clear The bald, white tumuli of your eyes. A blue sky out of the Oresteia Arches above us. O father, all by yourself You are pithy and historical as the Roman Forum. I open my lunch on a hill of black cypress. Your fluted bones and acanthine hair are littered In their old anarchy to the horizon-line. It would take more than a lightning-stroke To create such a ruin. Nights, I squat in the cornucopia Of your left ear, out of the wind, Counting the red stars and those of plum-color. The sun rises under the pillar of your tongue. My hours are married to shadow. No longer do I listen for the scrape of a keel On the blank stones of the landing.

outputs.L1:
This text is the celebrated poem **"The Colossus" by Sylvia Plath** (published in 1959). Because it is a foundational work of 20th-century poetry, altering its line breaks or vocabulary changes its artistic character. 

However, translating its intense imagery into an **eloquent, highly refined, and professional narrative prose version** (while preserving every original metaphor, detail, and meaning) yields the following adaptation:

***

> I despair of ever fully restoring you—reassembling, gluing, and properly joining your fragmented form. Only crude noises—the bray of a mule, the grunt of a pig, and raucous, vulgar cackles—emanate from your colossal lips; the tumult is worse than a barnyard. Perhaps you view yourself as a sacred oracle, a conduit for the voice of the dead or some distant deity. For thirty years now, I have labored to dredge the silt from your throat, yet I remain no wiser. 
> 
> Scaling miniature ladders equipped with pots of glue and pails of Lysol, I move like a grieving ant across the overgrown acres of your brow, working to repair your immense cranial plates and scour the smooth, white mounds of your eyes. Above us arches a stark blue sky reminiscent of the *Oresteia*. Father, in your solitary grandeur, you are as profound and historically monumental as the Roman Forum. 
> 
> I open my meal atop a hill of dark cypress, looking out over the landscape where your grooved bones and acanthine hair lie scattered in ancient chaos all the way to the horizon. It would require far more than a single bolt of lightning to create a ruin of such magnitude. 
> 
> At night, I take shelter from the wind within the curved cornucopia of your left ear, counting the stars that burn in shades of crimson and deep plum. The sun rises beneath the grand pillar of your tongue, and my days remain bound to shadow. I no longer listen for the scrape of a ship's keel against the featureless stones of the landing shore.
outputs.L2:
It will be impossible for me to ever fully rebuild you, fitting all your fragments together with adhesive and proper joints. From your gigantic lips issue coarse braying, swine-like grunts, and vulgar laughter—a racket far worse than any farmyard. You may imagine yourself to be a divine prophet or a speaker for the deceased. For three decades, I have worked tirelessly to clear the mud from your throat, yet I have gained no understanding. Carrying pots of paste and buckets of disinfectant up tiny ladders, I creep like a sorrowful insect across the vast, weed-covered expanse of your forehead, aiming to repair your colossal cranial plates and wash the smooth, pale mounds of your eyes.

An azure sky straight out of classical Greek tragedy curves over us. Father, in your solitary state, you hold as much rich historical weight as the Roman Forum. As I eat my meal among dark cypress trees, your grooved bones and spiky, leaf-like locks lie scattered in ancient chaos all the way to the horizon. Such immense devastation could not have been caused by a simple bolt of lightning.

During the night, I huddle safe from the breeze inside the horn-shaped shell of your left ear, tallying the crimson and purple stars above. Dawn breaks beneath the column supporting your tongue. My days are permanently tied to gloom, and I no longer strain my ears to catch the sound of a boat's hull scraping against the bare stone dock.
outputs.L3:
For decades, a singular and staggering labor has consumed my life: the tedious, meticulous attempt to clean, repair, and reassemble a chaotic, colossal figure. Scattered across a bleak landscape, its fractured limbs and shattered stone torso demand endless care. I have spent my best years clearing away debris, scrubbing lichen from its granite skin, and attempting to piece together a monumental puzzle whose original shape seems permanently lost to chaos.

Among the most grueling aspects of this lifelong effort has been the task of restoring the giant figure's voice. For thirty years, I labored under the belief that if I could only fix its cavernous throat, the being would impart profound revelations or ancient truths to justify my devotion. Yet, when sound finally emerged, it brought no wisdom or meaningful insight. The restored voice produced only raw, unintelligible noise—animalistic grunts and hollow reverberations that left me as uninformed and isolated as before. 

Despite this disappointment, the psychological bond remains unbreakable. I address this overwhelming, shattered monument as a mythical father figure, viewing its scattered remains through the lens of classical antiquity. Its broken limbs and cracked masonry resemble the ruins of an ancient civilization—its toes like overturned milestones, its torso like a collapsed Roman forum. It is a parent transformed into a ruin, monumental in scale yet completely broken.

Over time, my role has shifted from restorer to permanent inhabitant. I now physically dwell within the colossal structure itself, using its immense form for survival. When night falls and cold winds sweep across the wasteland, I crawl inside the sheltered curve of the giant’s massive ear to sleep. By day, I move across its vast surfaces, tending to the cracked, marble-like skin and scraping away the rot of time, domesticating my existence within the very disaster I sought to fix.

Ultimately, the drive to fully reconstruct the figure has dissolved into quiet resignation. Forever bound to the towering shadow of this immense ruin, I have accepted my total isolation. I no longer scan the distant horizon for passing ships, nor do I harbor any lingering hopes of rescue or escape. My world has shrunk entirely to the shadow of the fallen giant, where I remain tied to a history I can neither mend nor leave behind.
outputs.L4:
Thirty years ago, I dragged my first bucket of lime and iron scraper to the edge of the shore where he had fallen. He lay across the landscape not as a man, but as a shattered mountain—a ruin of pitted granite and cracked marble whose true dimensions could only be fathomed from the sky. His left thumb alone was the size of a sailing vessel; his broken brow rested half-buried in the silt, staring up at the clouds with blank, empty sockets. I was young then, naive enough to believe that a daughter’s devotion could reverse the devastation of time and gravity, and that by piecing him back together, I might finally understand the god who had sired me.

The work became the entire architecture of my life. For decades, my daily world was bounded by the tedious, backbreaking labor of restoration. I spent five years just clearing the lichen and salt-crust from his throat, crawling deep inside the dark, echoing cavern of his gullet with a hand-lantern to sweep out bird nests and windblown trash. I erected clumsy wooden scaffolds to reach his nose; I mixed barrel after barrel of pine-tar resin, mortar, and glue to mend the hairline fractures along his cheek. I hauled heavy pulleys across the rock face to hoist the knuckles of his right hand back into alignment, spending seasons polishing a single fingernail until it reflected the pale morning sun. 

My youth dissolved into the seams of his stone. My knuckles swelled to match his; my skin grew dry and grey, caked with the perpetual dust of his disintegrating frame. Yet, I persisted, sustained by a quiet, desperate faith that there would come a moment of revelation. I believed that once the jaw was seamlessly reattached to the skull, a rumble of ancient wisdom would echo from those colossal lips. I thought that when his chest was whole again, it would grant me a sense of order, a profound inheritance of peace, or at least a single syllable of paternal benediction to justify my bent spine and calloused hands.

Now, as the evening of my life sets in, the cruel truth of the endeavor has finally broken over me. The statue is too vast, the destruction too total. The weather erodes his brow faster than I can seal it, and the missing pieces—the fragments of his heart and mind that shattered into dust upon impact—can never be recovered. The jaw, though glued, remains mutely agape. No secret oracle lives within the granite. My decades of labor have bought me no warmth, no enlightenment, and no release. 

Today, I lay down my scraper and unbuckle my harness for the last time. I will never finish him. I retreat to the small, meager camp I have built between his thumb and his forefinger, exhausted and hollowed out. I am too old to leave, and there is nowhere else to go. The sun rises for the rest of the world, but here, in the cold, monolithic shade of his knee, it is forever twilight. I sit in the dark he creates, resigned to spend the rest of my days living beneath the heavy, inescapable weight of a monument that will never be whole.

The morning mist hung heavy over the ridge as Silas pulled gently on the reins of his steadfast **mule**, Barnaby. The animal snorted, its long ears twitching as it paused at the edge of the narrow, rocky pass. It was a stubborn beast, but in this treacherous terrain, Silas trusted the animal’s instincts far more than his own.

Reaching into his leather satchel, Silas pulled out a frayed map he had painstakingly **pieced** together from remnants of ancient parchment found in dusty port towns. Sketched lines of faded ink met at ragged edges, held in place by delicate strips of wax paper. He traced a finger across the stitched seam of the map, aligning the jagged silhouette of the distant peaks with the drawing in his hands.

Satisfied that they hadn't strayed from the old trade route, Silas stowed the map back into his bag and patted the animal's warm shoulder. The sun was finally breaking through the high canopy, casting long, golden streaks across the mountain path. With a quiet click of his tongue, Silas gave the signal to **proceed**, and together they stepped down into the shadowed valley below.

counterfactuals.prompt: Please provide the text of Sylvia Plath's poem "The Colossus".
counterfactuals.output:
Here is the text of Sylvia Plath's poem **"The Colossus"** (1960):

***

I shall never get you put together entirely,
Pieced, glued, and properly jointed.
Mule-bray, pig-grunt and several bawls
Proceed from your great lips.
It’s worse than a barnyard.

Perhaps you consider yourself an oracle,
Mouthpiece of the dead, or of some god or other.
Thirty years now I have labored
To dredge the silt from your throat.
I am none the wiser.

Scaling little ladders with my glue-pot and Lysol-can,
I crawl like an ant in mourning
Over the weedy acres of your brow
To mend the immense skull-plates and clear
The bald, white tumuli of your eyes.

A blue sky out of the Oresteia
Arches above us. O father, all by yourself
You are pithy and historical as the Roman Forum.
I open my lunch on a hill of beans.
Your fluted bones and acanthine hair are littered

In their cornucopia about the ridge.
It would take more than a lightning-strike
To ruin this ruin.
Nightly, I squat in the cornucopia
Of your left ear, out of the wind,

Counting the red stars and those of a plum-color.
The sun rises under the pillar of your tongue.
My hours are married to shadow.
No longer do I listen for the scrape of a keel
On the blank stones of the landing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, confessional poem about a woman painstakingly trying to glue together a giant, ruined statue of her father.
counterfactuals.output:
He lies across four acres of my overgrown yard,
his left ear a crater where blue jays nest.
I move between his severed limbs with a bucket of epoxy
and a spatulate butter knife,
my apron stiffened with cured resin and white dust.

Forgive me. I made you this large.
When I was seven, you blocked the sun;
by twenty, you were a mountain I had to dynamite
just to see the horizon.
Now you are a landslide of alabaster and cold iron,
and I am knee-deep in your knuckles,
trying to find where the thumb meets the wrist.

I dragged your nose—a five-ton wedge of granite—
using a harness hitched around my chest.
My knees are purple bruised, my spine a warped nail.
I apply three drops of Krazy Glue to the bridge
and hold it against your face for forty minutes,
breathing in the smell of calcified tobacco and old rain
that still leaks from your pores.

When the seam fails, your cheek drops,
crushing my flowerbeds,
opening a hollow cavern in your head where a choir
of feral cats now lives, singing hymns in the dark.

*I am doing this because I broke you first,* I tell the grass.
*I am doing this because if you aren't towering, I am just alone.*

At noon, I climb a rope ladder into your chest cavity.
It smells of rusted gears and dried peppermint.
I apply thick paste to the fracture in your sternum,
pasting my own hair into the fissures to act as binder.
My skin peels off against your stone chin,
leaving pink tape behind. We are merging.
I am becoming the mortar for a man who never asked to be built.

Tonight, the wind will come up from the valley.
The adhesive will cure incorrectly, distorted by my warm, wet hands.
By dawn, your left shoulder will snap off again,
crashing through the roof of the greenhouse.

And I will get up with my little tube,
my butter knife, my bucket of spit and glue,
and walk out into the fog
to match the gravel on the driveway
to the broken, silent puzzle of your smile.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem in the style of Sylvia Plath that explores themes of grief, myth, and an overwhelming father figure?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Marble Titan**

You lie spread across the headland, a broken colossus,  
Your granite toes dipping into the Atlantic.  
The salt eats at your kneecaps; barnacles crown your brow.  
I am the small, black beetle crawling your lip,  
Trying to scrape the lichen from your teeth.  
Thirty years I have lived in the shadow of your knee,  
A tiny Persephone waiting for the sun you swallowed.  

You were Kronos in a heavy wool coat,  
Smelling of tobacco, peat, and formaldehyde.  
When you spoke, the glass shattered in the pantry,  
The milk curdled in its blue ceramic jug.  
You carried the mountains in your waistcoat pocket  
And left me only the gravel,  
The grey grit to chew on in the dark.  

I have tried to put you back together.  
With glue and marine solder, I patch your marble ribs,  
I haul the heavy anvil of your heart out of the surf.  
O Goliath, the tide comes in to drown your empty sockets,  
And I am left treading the black, cold water of your silence.  
Your absence is an iron lung,  
Pumping the air out of my room.  

In my dreams, you are Atlas, unbending,  
Dropping the sky straight onto my shoulders.  
The stars are sharp bits of gravel in my eye.  
I dig through the peat, looking for your leather boots,  
Looking for the voice that flattened the daisies,  
The great red mouth that breathed the frost.  

I am tired of scraping the lime from your jaw.  
I am tired of dining on the cold stone of your memory.  
The sea roars in your earholes, heavy and deaf,  
And still, your dead hand reaches out from the tide,  
A massive claw,  
Pinning me down to the sand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem beginning with the line: "I shall never get you put together entirely," using classical references like the Oresteia and the Roman Forum.
counterfactuals.output:
I shall never get you put together entirely,
strewn like cracked marble across the grass,
or scattered down the cobbles of the Via Sacra
where emperor and captive used to pass.
I sift through the dust of the Roman Forum,
searching for the frieze that held your face—
a torso fallen from a triumphal arch,
drowned in wild ivy and time’s erase.

You are a ruin older than these Latin stones,
echoing the blood-heavy halls of Argos.
In the shadow of your ribs, I hear the chorus wail 
for Agamemnon, struck down in his bath,
while Clytemnestra waits with red carpets laid.
You carry the ancient curse of Atreus in your marrow,
a splintered legacy no mortal hands can mend,
haunted by the Furies who hound your broken tracks
demanding vengeance that will never end.

I hold a fragment of your shattered brow to the light—
is it a sculpted leaf of Corinthian acanthus,
or the memory of an unforgotten fright?
Not even the cast pebbles at the Areopagus,
where Athena hushed the snake-haired Eumenides,
could weigh your fragments into harmony again.
The court of gods has long since gone to sleep,
leaving only silence and the cypress trees.

So rest in your magnificently shattered state.
The sun sinks low across the Palatine Hill,
casting giant shadows over temple, arch, and gate.
I drop the last small piece into the dirt,
learning to love the ruin as it stands:
unfinished, tragic, colossal, and still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: I'm looking for a poem about the futile, lifelong labor of trying to understand a dead parent, framed through the metaphor of cleaning and assembling a colossal stone monument.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Colossus at Forty**

He fell in silence, leaving only the quarry—
a mountain of granite scattered in the high grass,
a head the size of a chapel, a chest like a wall,
and the cold, unyielding mass of his history.

I was young when I bought the scaffolding.
I brought my iron chisels, my vinegar, my wire rags.
I promised myself I would scrub away the centuries of silt,
would haul the heavy limbs back to their joints,
would stand him upright against the sky
so I might finally look him in the eye.

For forty years, this has been my altar and my chore.
I spend my mornings scraping lichen from his ear,
hoping to find the ear-canal, the secret passage
to whatever quiet thought he kept from me.
I polish the stone coat until it gleams like oil,
yet by evening, the sea-wind bakes it dull again.

The assembly is the hardest part.
With ropes and winches, my hands bleeding into the hemp,
I dragged his massive left shoulder toward the neck.
It fits, but only almost.
A jagged gap remains—a hollow three feet wide—
where his boyhood should have been.
I have searched the valley for that missing piece,
but it was ground to dust before I was born.

Now my own knees ache when the damp sets in.
My hair turns the color of the slate I sweep.
I realize the cruelty of the geometry:
while I polish his left cheek to a mirror’s sheen,
the right cheek, unattended, grows black with moss. 
I am losing ground to the weather.

I will die here, at the base of his giant, unmoving heel,
a small man holding a bucket of water and a sponge.
He will remain as he always was—
vast, fragmented, impossibly heavy,
and completely blind,
staring out over the head of the son 
who broke his life trying to rebuild him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
